items.title: NSA Releases 1966 Secret Study on “Coupon Collecting and Cryptology” After Nine-Year FOIA Wait
items.summary: A mathematical study published inside the National Security Agency six decades ago has been released through the Freedom of Information Act, more than nine years after The Black Vault requested it. The paper, “Coupon Collecting and Cryptology,” was written by Marie Capozza and published in the Fall 1966 edition of the NSA Technical Journal. Although the title had been publicly identified for years in declassified indexes of NSA publications, searches conducted by The Black Vault did not locate a previously public copy of the paper itself. The 1966 study released in response to the FOIA request therefore provides a newly available look at how NSA mathematicians examined a classic probability problem and applied it to cryptologic questions. The Black Vault requested the article from NSA on August 6, 2017. NSA’s response is dated September 9, 2026, more than nine years later. The agency released the responsive document with portions withheld under FOIA Exemptions 1 and 3. Despite its complex pages of equations, the basic idea behind the paper is relatively straightforward: If items are selected randomly from a fixed number of possible types, how long should it take before every type has appeared; and can deviations from that expected behavior reveal that the selection process is not actually random? For the NSA, that question had direct applications to cryptology. From Cereal-Box Coupons to Cryptology Capozza begins with a deliberately ordinary example. “Let us assume that a…

items.title: NSA Located a Classified QAnon-Related Record — All Three Pages Were Withheld
items.summary: A Freedom of Information Act request seeking National Security Agency records mentioning or cross-referencing QAnon has produced a limited set of material: an internal employee discussion in which QAnon was invoked casually as a joke, records associated with an earlier FOIA request filed by The Black Vault, and, more significantly, confirmation that the NSA located a separate three-page document that remains classified SECRET and was withheld in its entirety. The NSA’s March 25, 2026, response concerned a FOIA request filed on February 10, 2020, seeking records that “pertain or mention or contain cross references to QAnon.” The request covered records dating from 2016 through the date the request was processed. The response does not disclose the subject, origin, date or contents of the three-page classified record. Consequently, the release provides no basis to conclude what connection the withheld document has to QAnon. It could contain a substantive discussion of the movement, a passing reference, a cross-reference comparable to the material that was released, or something else entirely. The available record does not resolve that question. A SECRET Document Withheld in Full According to the NSA, “1 document (3 pages) has been withheld in its entirety.” The agency said the document remains properly classified under Executive Order 13526 and specifically cited Sections 1.4(c) and 1.4(g). items.title: Behind AARO’s Private UAP Workshop: New Records Detail Participants, Foreign Outreach and Future Plans
items.summary: A newly released collection of records from the Pentagon’s All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office provides a substantially more detailed look at the government-sponsored UAP research workshop held outside Washington, D.C., in August 2025, including a working agenda identifying speakers and panelists, previously unreleased correspondence concerning foreign participation, and evidence that AARO was already discussing a follow-on workshop months before the first event took place. The records also document a separate Pentagon engagement with representatives of Uruguay’s official UAP investigative organization, including plans for reciprocal mission briefings, discussions about future collaboration, lunch with senior AARO personnel and a private Pentagon tour. The documents were released to The Black Vault under Freedom of Information Act case 26-F-1773. The request was filed March 17, 2026, one day after DefenseScoop senior reporter Brandi Vincent broke the story of the invitation-only workshop and obtained additional information about it from the Pentagon. Vincent’s original reporting established that approximately 40 government, academic and independent researchers had participated in the AARO-sponsored gathering and detailed its emphasis on integrating narrative UAP data and applying artificial intelligence to large datasets. The new FOIA release does not fundamentally alter the publicly stated purpose or findings of the workshop. Instead, its significance is in filling in…

items.title: Navy Releases Massive Cache of Scott Bray UAP Emails After Four Years; More Than 300 Pages Withheld in Full
items.summary: The Department of the Navy has released more than 1,300 pages of emails and related records involving former Deputy Director of Naval Intelligence Scott W. Bray, opening a broad window into government communications surrounding unidentified aerial phenomena during a pivotal period in the Pentagon’s modern UAP effort. The records were obtained by The Black Vault through a Freedom of Information Act request filed on May 24, 2022. The request sought emails sent to, from, copied to or blind-copied to Bray containing terms including “Unidentified Aerial Phenomena,” “UAP,” “UAPTF,” “UFO,” “AATIP,” “AAWSAP” and several related phrases. More than four years later, the Navy responded on September 23, 2026. According to its response, the search located 1,321 pages of responsive records. The Navy withheld 302 pages in their entirety, while releasing the remaining 1,019 pages with redactions under several FOIA exemptions. Who Was Scott Bray? Bray served as Deputy Director of Naval Intelligence and Director of the Naval Intelligence Activity during much of the period covered by the records. His position placed him within a network of Navy, Defense Department and Intelligence Community officials dealing with UAP reporting, briefings, congressional interest and the development of what ultimately became the Navy-led Unidentified Aerial Phenomena Task Force. items.title: Inside Jeffrey Epstein’s CIA Privacy Act Requests for Records About Himself
items.summary: Newly released Central Intelligence Agency records provide the most complete look yet at two separate attempts by Jeffrey Epstein, which were more than a decade apart, to determine what information the CIA maintained about him. The records were obtained by The Black Vault after case numbers for Epstein’s Privacy Act requests surfaced within the broader government release of Epstein-related files. Rather than requesting CIA records about Epstein specifically, The Black Vault used those case identifiers, listed as P-1999-02450 and P-2011-00673, to seek the records generated during the processing of the two cases. This also stemmed from a public call to action request from political commentator and speechwriter Mike Benz. The CIA responded on September 18, 2026, under FOIA case F-2026-00889, saying it had located 17 responsive documents. One was released in full and 16 were released with portions withheld under FOIA Exemptions (b)(3) and/or (b)(6). The resulting near 50-page release contains Epstein’s original 1999 request, internal CIA search records, correspondence between Epstein and the agency, and the records surrounding a substantially more specific request submitted on his behalf in 2011. The documents establish that the CIA reported finding no records filed under Epstein’s name in response to his first request. In 2011, the agency similarly reported finding no records reflecting an open or otherwise acknowledged CIA affiliation during the period it searched. For records…

Often dubbed “Pennsylvania’s Roswell,” it involved reports of a fiery fireball streaking over several U.S. states and Canada, a crash in the woods near the village of Kecksburg, and an alleged military recovery of an unknown object [1] . As someone who has been impersonated by AI daily on large video platforms for a few years now, I have come to acutely feel that AI is becoming a dangerous force that is making it increasingly difficult for well-meaning readers/viewers to distinguish between what is real and what is false. I don’t mean just for those hoping to view my content, as the personal issue I am facing is a microcosm of a much larger problem. As a result, one might think that I would have been pleased, if not relieved, to see Substack, a large platform for professional writers, partner with an “AI detection tool.” Not only am I not pleased, but I have now taken the time to write an opinion piece explaining why I think this is bad and to also explain where I think a lot of this is going. Substack’s new partner and, apparently, the AI detection tool of choice for most major media outlets right now is called Pangram. Pangram was founded in 2023, originally under the name Checkfor.ai, by Max Spero and Bradley Emi.
